newsitem.title: USA: Ill. COPs suit settlement may spur refinancings.
newsitem.headline: Ill. COPs suit settlement may spur refinancings.

text.p: A proposed settlement of a lawsuit challenging the state's use of certificates of participation to fund an office building project may spur numerous refinancings of recent issues as well, a state lawmaker who brought the claim said Wednesday.

The settlement between Gov. Jim Edgar and a handful of state lawmakers also would require the governor to sign a bill that restricts and accounts for the use of certificates for improvements to real property, Rep. Jeffrey Schoenberg, D-Evanston, said.

Schoenberg and other House Democrats filed the lawsuit in June 1996 contending that the state Department of Central Management Services exceeded its authority by issuing $19.2 million of certificates of participation (COPs) in a lease-purchase agreement for new public aid building in downtown Chicago.

The settlement would give the state budget bureau express authority to refinance the COPs issues through general obligation bonds and requires the conversion "under appropriate circumstances," Schoenberg said.

A draft of the settlement states that the budget bureau would be required to determine if the state should refinance COPs issued for construction of an Illinois Student Assistance Commission building in north suburban Deerfield.

The state issued $23.9 million of COPs in March 1992 for student assistance building and an analysis by Dougherty Dawkins Inc showed that Illinois could save nearly $1 million if they were reissued as general obligation bonds, Schoenberg said.

A number of other COPs issues could be refinanced, including $33.15 million of COPs issued for the construction of an Illinois Environmental Protection Agency building in Springfield in April 1996, Schoenberg said.

The settlement also requires continued negotiations with the governor's office for other state procurement reforms in the fall veto session and requires the state to pay $45,000 in legal fees to plaintiffs' attorney Edmund Moran.
Several weeks of negotiations in May intensified near the close of the legislative session, leading to a tentative agreement, Schoenberg said.
A written agreement was distributed Tuesday and the case could be dismissed later this week, Schoenberg added.

Schoenberg, chairman of the House appropriations committee, said his committee did not approve legislation for a fiscal 1998 payment on the public aid building COPs issue until after completion of the tentative agreement.

Moody's Investors Service had indicated that failure to pay the debt service would have negative consequences and it would have been "fiscally irresponsible to imperil the state's bond rating," Schoenberg said.
